claim: Crossed-corticostriatal (CCS) 'slender untufted' pyramidal cells are a discrete neuronal population in layer V of rat frontal cortex
source: Crossed-corticostriatal (CCS) 'slender untufted' pyramidal cells (Larkman and Mason, 1990 Morishima and Kawaguchi, 2006) are a discrete neuronal population in L5.
evidence: Supported by citations to Larkman and Mason, 1990 and Morishima and Kawaguchi, 2006

claim: CCS pyramidal cells were identified by injecting a fluorescent retrograde tracer into the contralateral striatum
source: We investigated connections between FS basket cells and CCS pyramidal cells, identified by injecting a fluorescent retrograde tracer into the contralateral striatum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental method described in text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: IPSCs reversed on average at −52.5 mV in CCS pyramidal cells held at −65 mV
source: With pyramidal cell membrane potential maintained at −65 mV, IPSCs reversed on average at −52.5 mV (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), providing a mean driving force of 12.5 mV.
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: The mean driving force for IPSCs was 12.5 mV
source: With pyramidal cell membrane potential maintained at −65 mV, IPSCs reversed on average at −52.5 mV (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), providing a mean driving force of 12.5 mV.
evidence: Calculated from the difference between holding potential and reversal potential

claim: Paired recordings were made from neighboring cells with inter-somatic distance of 44.5 ± 23.7 µm (range 20.6–66.6 µm, n = 10)
source: Paired recordings were made from neighboring cells (Table 1, inter-somatic distance: 44.5 ± 23.7 µm, 20.6–66.6 µm, n = 10).
evidence: Experimental measurements reported in Table 1

claim: There was typically a large overlap of the basal dendrites of postsynaptic pyramidal cells and the axonal arbor of presynaptic FS basket cells
source: There was typically a large overlap of the basal dendrites of postsynaptic pyramidal cells and the axonal arbor of presynaptic FS basket cells (Figure 1B,G, Figure 2B,G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Morphological observation shown in multiple figures

claim: In three cell pairs, FS basket cell axons established putative synaptic contacts on the soma and dendrites of postsynaptic CCS pyramidal cells
source: In three cell pairs, FS basket cell axons established putative synaptic contacts on the soma and dendrites of a postsynaptic CCS pyramidal cell (Figure 1J, upper three lines).
evidence: Morphological analysis shown in Figure 1J

claim: In seven pairs, synaptic contacts were located exclusively on dendrites at various distances from the soma
source: In seven pairs, synaptic contacts were located exclusively on dendrites at various distances from the soma (Figure 1J, lower 7 lines).
evidence: Morphological analysis shown in Figure 1J

claim: The number of putative synaptic contacts was 5–14 (8.2 ± 4.8, 10 pairs)
source: The number of putative synaptic contacts was 5–14 (8.2 ± 4.8, 10 pairs).
evidence: Quantitative morphological analysis from 10 cell pairs

claim: Most light microscopic contacts were made where FS basket cell axons crossed basal pyramidal cell dendrites
source: Most light microscopic contacts were made where FS basket cell axons crossed basal pyramidal cell dendrites (Figure 1D,E,H,I, Figure 2D,I, Figure 3B) (Marlin and Carter, 2014).
evidence: Morphological observation shown in figures and supported by citation

claim: The distance from the soma to dendritic contacts was 5.8–208.4 µm with a mean value of 82.5 ± 50.0 µm
source: The distance from the soma to dendritic contacts was 5.8–208.4 µm with a mean value of 82.5 ± 50.0 µm.
evidence: Quantitative morphological measurements

claim: Peak IPSC amplitude was larger in pairs with putative somatic contacts than those when contacts were exclusively dendritic
source: Peak IPSC amplitude was larger in pairs with putative somatic contacts than those when contacts were exclusively dendritic (Figure 1J).
evidence: Electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 1J

claim: Transmission never failed for pairs with somatic contacts but failures occurred with dendritic contacts
source: Transmission never failed for pairs with somatic contacts but failures occurred with dendritic contacts (Table 1).
evidence: Electrophysiological data reported in Table 1

claim: Mean IPSC amplitude from pairs with only dendritic contacts was reduced at increasing distances from the soma to the nearest contact
source: Mean IPSC amplitude, from pairs with only dendritic contacts, was reduced at increasing distances from the soma to the nearest contact (Figure 1J).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 1J

claim: IPSCs were not detected in two pairs where light microscopy suggested 7 and 9 contacts were made at distances further than 33 µm from the soma
source: IPSCs were not detected in two pairs, where light microscopy (LM) suggested 7 and 9 contacts were made at distances further than 33 µm from the soma (Figure 1J, lower 2 lines).
evidence: Electrophysiological and morphological data shown in Figure 1J

claim: Serial electron micrograph reconstructions showed that somatic synapses were larger than dendritic contacts
source: Serial electron micrograph (EMg) reconstructions showed that somatic synapses were larger than dendritic contacts.
evidence: EM analysis results stated in abstract

claim: FS cell soma-targeting synapses initiate a strong, global inhibition
source: FS cell soma-targeting synapses initiate a strong, global inhibition, those on shafts inhibit more restricted dendritic zones, while synapses on spines may mediate a strictly local veto.
evidence: Conclusion from simulations with anatomical and physiological data

claim: FS cell synapses on dendritic shafts inhibit more restricted dendritic zones
source: FS cell soma-targeting synapses initiate a strong, global inhibition, those on shafts inhibit more restricted dendritic zones, while synapses on spines may mediate a strictly local veto.
evidence: Conclusion from simulations with anatomical and physiological data

claim: FS cell synapses on spines may mediate a strictly local veto
source: FS cell soma-targeting synapses initiate a strong, global inhibition, those on shafts inhibit more restricted dendritic zones, while synapses on spines may mediate a strictly local veto.
evidence: Conclusion from simulations with anatomical and physiological data

claim: FS cell synapses of different sizes and sites provide functionally diverse forms of pyramidal cell inhibition
source: Thus, FS cell synapses of different sizes and sites provide functionally diverse forms of pyramidal cell inhibition.
evidence: Main conclusion from combined anatomical, physiological, and simulation data

claim: Inhibitory interneurons target precise membrane regions on pyramidal cells
source: Inhibitory interneurons target precise membrane regions on pyramidal cells, but differences in their functional effects on somata, dendrites and spines remain unclear.
evidence: Established knowledge stated as background

claim: Inhibitory synapses target multiple membrane domains of pyramidal cells: soma, axon initial segment, dendritic shafts and spines
source: However, mechanisms controlling inhibitory synaptic actions are incompletely understood. For instance, inhibitory synapses target multiple membrane domains of pyramidal cells: soma, axon initial segment, dendritic shafts and spines (Kisvarday et al., 1985; Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1998; Szabadics et al., 2006; Kubota et al., 2007; Jiang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Contacts at different sites produce inhibitory postsynaptic potentials with different properties
source: Contacts at these different sites produce inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSP) with different properties (Miles et al., 1996; Xue et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Miles et al., 1996 and Xue et al., 2014

claim: IPSCs generated by FS basket cells may be matched to the level of synaptic excitation in cortical pyramidal cells
source: Recent data suggests IPSCs generated by FS basket cells may be matched to the level of synaptic excitation in cortical pyramidal cells (Xue et al., 2014), and differ with target cell subtypes (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xue et al., 2014

claim: IPSCs generated by FS basket cells differ with target cell subtypes
source: Recent data suggests IPSCs generated by FS basket cells may be matched to the level of synaptic excitation in cortical pyramidal cells (Xue et al., 2014), and differ with target cell subtypes (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2014

claim: Unitary inhibitory postsynaptic currents are significantly smaller in neurons of Disc1 mice, a genetic model of depression
source: Unitary inhibitory postsynaptic currents (uIPSCs) are significantly smaller in neurons of Disc1 mice, a genetic model of depression, and may underlie reduced low-gamma oscillations in the frontal cortex (Sauer et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sauer et al., 2015

claim: Reduced uIPSCs in Disc1 mice may underlie reduced low-gamma oscillations in the frontal cortex
source: Unitary inhibitory postsynaptic currents (uIPSCs) are significantly smaller in neurons of Disc1 mice, a genetic model of depression, and may underlie reduced low-gamma oscillations in the frontal cortex (Sauer et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative connection supported by citation to Sauer et al., 2015

claim: GABA receptors on spine heads are thought to control local synaptic excitation
source: GABA receptors on spine heads are thought to control local synaptic excitation (Chiu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chiu et al., 2013

claim: Modeling studies assume that somatic, dendritic shaft and spine inhibition is mediated by pre-synaptic elements of identical size and strength
source: Modeling studies assume that somatic, dendritic shaft and spine inhibition is mediated by pre-synaptic elements of identical size and strength (Gidon and Segev, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gidon and Segev, 2012

claim: Excitatory synaptic terminals vary in size and their strength is correlated with terminal size
source: In contrast, excitatory synaptic terminals vary in size and their strength is correlated with terminal size (Holderith et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holderith et al., 2012

claim: For pair CS56, 3 of 7 possible contacts were verified by EM, but no synaptic contact was made at 4 other potential sites
source: EM analysis let us verify possible synaptic contacts from LM. For the pair CS56, 3 of 7 possible contacts were verified by EM, but no synaptic contact was made at 4 other potential sites (Figure 4).
evidence: EM verification results shown in Figure 4

claim: One putative LM contact was resolved as three distinct en passant boutons (S1–S3)
source: One putative LM contact was resolved as three distinct en passant boutons (S1–S3 in Figure 5A–E) and another somatic contact was detected only by EM (S4, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: EM analysis shown in Figure 5A–E

claim: For pair CS56, the junctional area of somatic synapses was 0.194–0.350 µm2
source: For somatic synapses junctional area was 0.194–0.350 µm2, it was 0.102 µm2 for synapses with dendritic shafts and 0.042–0.056 µm2 for synapses onto spine heads (Figure 6F, Table 2).
evidence: EM measurements shown in Figure 6F and Table 2

claim: For pair CS56, the junctional area of dendritic shaft synapses was 0.102 µm2
source: For somatic synapses junctional area was 0.194–0.350 µm2, it was 0.102 µm2 for synapses with dendritic shafts and 0.042–0.056 µm2 for synapses onto spine heads (Figure 6F, Table 2).
evidence: EM measurements shown in Figure 6F and Table 2

claim: For pair CS56, the junctional area of spine head synapses was 0.042–0.056 µm2
source: For somatic synapses junctional area was 0.194–0.350 µm2, it was 0.102 µm2 for synapses with dendritic shafts and 0.042–0.056 µm2 for synapses onto spine heads (Figure 6F, Table 2).
evidence: EM measurements shown in Figure 6F and Table 2

claim: Axonal bouton volume was linearly correlated with synaptic junction area
source: Axonal bouton volume was linearly correlated with synaptic junction area (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: Injecting a 0.11 nS current on the spine head of Sp1 resulted in a strong 0.78 mV hyperpolarization of the spine, but only 0.12 mV was transmitted to the basal dendrite and 0.07 mV to the soma
source: Injecting a 0.11 nS current on the spine head of Sp1 (Table 2) resulted in a strong 0.78 mV hyperpolarization of the spine, but only 0.12 mV was transmitted to the basal dendrite and 0.07 mV to the soma (Figure 8A,C,K).
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figure 8A,C,K

claim: The spine neck effectively isolated the spine head from the dendritic shaft with neck length 0.5 µm, diameter 0.07 µm, volume 0.043 µm3, and resistance 500 MΩ
source: The spine neck effectively isolated the spine head from the dendritic shaft (neck length, 0.5 µm; diameter, 0.07 µm; volume, 0.043 µm3; resistance, 500 MΩ [Harnett et al., 2012]).
evidence: Simulation parameters based on citation to Harnett et al., 2012

claim: Spine inhibition did not change nearby dendritic shaft or somatic potential
source: Thus spine inhibition did not change nearby dendritic shaft or somatic potential (Araya et al., 2006).
evidence: Simulation result supported by citation to Araya et al., 2006

claim: Injecting a 0.21 nS synaptic current on the dendritic shaft (D1) caused a hyperpolarization of 0.23 mV on the shaft and 0.13 mV at the soma
source: In contrast, injecting a 0.21 nS synaptic current on the dendritic shaft (D1) (Table 2) caused a hyperpolarization of 0.23 mV on the shaft and 0.13 mV at the soma (Figure 8D,F,K).
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figure 8D,F,K

claim: Injecting a synaptic waveform of 0.71 nS at the soma (S1) hyperpolarized that site by 0.48 mV
source: Injecting a synaptic waveform of 0.71 nS at the soma (S1) (Table 2) hyperpolarized that site by 0.48 mV (Figure 8G,H) resulting in an IPSC of 8.29 pA (Figure 8H), in the range of background noise.
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figure 8G,H

claim: Simultaneous activation of somatic contacts S1–S4 resulted in a hyperpolarization of 1.33 mV, corresponding to a somatic current of 22.67 pA
source: Simultaneous activation of somatic contacts S1–S4 resulted in a hyperpolarization of 1.33 mV, corresponding to a somatic current of 22.67 pA, (Figure 8I,J) similar to IPSP amplitudes from paired recordings of FS basket cells to hippocampal pyramidal cells (0.5–3 mV) (Buhl et al., 1994) and our own data (Figure 2E, Table 5).
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figure 8I,J and compared to literature

claim: For a similar driving force, proximal inhibitory synapses produce larger somatic hyperpolarizations than distal ones
source: Thus for a similar driving force, proximal inhibitory synapses produce larger somatic hyperpolarizations than distal ones (Figure 8K).
evidence: Conclusion from simulation results shown in Figure 8K

claim: Excitatory synaptic events (0.2 nS) at spine heads were greatly reduced by a coincident spine-head IPSC
source: Excitatory synaptic events (0.2 nS) were greatly reduced by a coincident spine-head IPSC (Figure 8L).
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figure 8L

claim: Inhibition from clustered somatic synapses of one FS basket cell effectively suppressed dendro-somatic conduction of inputs from approximately 11 excitatory spine synapses
source: Thus inhibition from clustered somatic synapses of one FS basket cell effectively suppressed dendro-somatic conduction of inputs from ∼11 excitatory spine synapses.
evidence: Calculated from simulation results comparing inhibitory and excitatory effects

claim: The unit electrical charge was 343.3 fC µm−2 for pair CS56
source: The unit electrical charge was calculated as the maximum charge divided by the summed junction area of S1–S4: 326.1 fC/0.95 µm2, or, 343.3 fC µm−2 for pair CS56, and S1–S13, D1–D4, Sp1–Sp4: 1057.8 fC/3.011 µm2, or 351.3 fC µm−2 for pair CS55 (Table 6).
evidence: Calculated from experimental measurements in Table 6

claim: The unit electrical charge was 351.3 fC µm−2 for pair CS55
source: The unit electrical charge was calculated as the maximum charge divided by the summed junction area of S1–S4: 326.1 fC/0.95 µm2, or, 343.3 fC µm−2 for pair CS56, and S1–S13, D1–D4, Sp1–Sp4: 1057.8 fC/3.011 µm2, or 351.3 fC µm−2 for pair CS55 (Table 6).
evidence: Calculated from experimental measurements in Table 6

claim: Unit IPSCs from recordings were quite similar between pairs CS56 and CS55, suggesting that the inhibitory synaptic current is well correlated with synaptic junction area
source: Surprisingly unit IPSCs from recordings in this work were quite similar, suggesting that the inhibitory synaptic current is well correlated with synaptic junction area.
evidence: Inference from comparison of unit electrical charge values

claim: 28.4 ± 7.6% (17.2–43.1%) of FS interneuron terminals contacted cell somata
source: From all paired records, 28.4 ± 7.6% (17.2–43.1%) of FS interneuron terminals contacted cell somata (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, Table 4), consistent with previous data (Karube et al., 2004).
evidence: Quantitative analysis shown in Table 4 and consistent with citation

claim: An FS cell that innervates only dendrites of one L5 pyramidal cell may contact somatic sites of other postsynaptic neurons
source: We note that an FS cell that innervates only dendrites of one L5 pyramidal cell, may contact somatic sites of other postsynaptic neurons (Figure 7).
evidence: Observation from morphological analysis shown in Figure 7

claim: IPSC amplitude variations result from an independent, stochastic activation of individual somatic and proximal synapses
source: IPSC charge distributions from paired recordings and simulations were statistically similar (p = 0.41 Kolmogorov–Smirnov, Figure 8N,P), suggesting that IPSC amplitude variations result from an independent, stochastic activation of individual somatic and proximal synapses (Sasaki et al., 2012).
evidence: Statistical comparison of experimental and simulation data with citation support

claim: The junctional area of somatic inhibitory synapses was 0.40 ± 0.15 μm2 (n = 23) across 9 different types of interneuron
source: The junctional area of somatic inhibitory synapses was 0.40 ± 0.15 μm2 (n = 23), for dendritic shaft synapses it was 0.19 ± 0.12 μm2 (n = 195) and for synapses terminating on spines it was 0.09 ± 0.05 μm2 (n = 87).
evidence: EM measurements from 305 synapses made by 9 different types of interneuron

claim: The junctional area of dendritic shaft inhibitory synapses was 0.19 ± 0.12 μm2 (n = 195) across 9 different types of interneuron
source: The junctional area of somatic inhibitory synapses was 0.40 ± 0.15 μm2 (n = 23), for dendritic shaft synapses it was 0.19 ± 0.12 μm2 (n = 195) and for synapses terminating on spines it was 0.09 ± 0.05 μm2 (n = 87).
evidence: EM measurements from 305 synapses made by 9 different types of interneuron

claim: The junctional area of spine inhibitory synapses was 0.09 ± 0.05 μm2 (n = 87) across 9 different types of interneuron
source: The junctional area of somatic inhibitory synapses was 0.40 ± 0.15 μm2 (n = 23), for dendritic shaft synapses it was 0.19 ± 0.12 μm2 (n = 195) and for synapses terminating on spines it was 0.09 ± 0.05 μm2 (n = 87).
evidence: EM measurements from 305 synapses made by 9 different types of interneuron

claim: Synaptic junctional area was correlated with the size of the target structure
source: Synaptic junctional area was therefore correlated with the size of the target structure (Figure 10B–L) with the possible exception of Martinotti cell terminals (Figure 10J) that contact distal pyramidal cell dendrites (Silberberg and Markram, 2007).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 10B–L with citation for Martinotti cells

claim: Linear relations between synapse junction and post-synaptic target size may provide an effective impedance matching
source: Linear relations between synapse junction and post-synaptic target size (Figure 10B–L) may provide an effective impedance matching (Kubota and Kawaguchi, 2000) and thus control the inhibitory efficacy at different sites.
evidence: Interpretation of correlation data with citation support

claim: The variation in effects of FS basket cell synapses targeting different membrane regions on L5 pyramidal cells may reflect a general principle for inhibitory cortical circuits
source: Thus the variation in effects of FS basket cell synapses targeting different membrane regions on L5 pyramidal cells may reflects a general principle for inhibitory cortical circuits.
evidence: Generalization from data across multiple interneuron types

claim: FS basket cells mediate either a global somatic inhibition of variable strength, a local dendritic shaft inhibition or act as a local veto at single spines
source: These data show that FS basket cells mediate either a global somatic inhibition of variable strength, a local dendritic shaft inhibition or act as a local veto at single spines.
evidence: Main conclusion from combined experimental and simulation data

claim: Local spine or shaft potential changes are small and locally restricted
source: Local spine or shaft potential changes are small and locally restricted.
evidence: Conclusion from simulation results

claim: Somatic inhibitory currents are large, and summation of events from several somatic terminals produces a global control of pyramidal cell excitation
source: In contrast, somatic inhibitory currents are large, and summation of events from several somatic terminals produces a global control of pyramidal cell excitation.
evidence: Conclusion from simulation and experimental results

claim: Somatic junctions have large areas, suggesting high release probability
source: Somatic junctions have large areas, suggesting high release probability (Holderith et al., 2012) and typically contact multiple sites (Buhl et al., 1994).

claim: Somatic junctions typically contact multiple sites
source: Somatic junctions have large areas, suggesting high release probability (Holderith et al., 2012) and typically contact multiple sites (Buhl et al., 1994).
evidence: Morphological observation supported by citation to Buhl et al., 1994

claim: FS cells fire repetitively at 30–50 Hz during motor behaviors in vivo
source: This enhances the likelihood of simultaneous release as FS cells fire repetitively at 30–50 Hz during motor behaviors in vivo (Isomura et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Isomura et al., 2009

claim: Some FS basket cell connections with pyramidal cells involved exclusively dendritic sites while others consisted of both peri-somatic and proximal dendritic contacts
source: Some FS basket cell connections with pyramidal cells involved exclusively dendritic sites while others consisted of both peri-somatic and proximal dendritic contacts.
evidence: Morphological observation from paired recordings

claim: Spines receiving inhibitory synapses are typically large
source: Spines receiving inhibitory synapses are typically large (Kubota et al., 2007) and their thalamic excitatory inputs presumably express both NMDA and AMPA receptors (Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Kubota et al., 2007).

claim: Thalamic excitatory inputs to spines receiving inhibitory synapses presumably express both NMDA and AMPA receptors
source: Spines receiving inhibitory synapses are typically large (Kubota et al., 2007) and their thalamic excitatory inputs presumably express both NMDA and AMPA receptors (Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Kubota et al., 2007).

claim: Inhibitory synapses may efficiently veto thalamic inputs before activation of NMDA receptors
source: Inhibitory synapses may then efficiently veto these thalamic inputs before activation of NMDA receptors (Gulledge et al., 2012) so reducing the probability of pyramidal cell firing.

claim: In paired recordings IPSCs were detected only for terminals that contacted proximal pyramidal cell dendrites
source: In paired recordings IPSCs were detected only for terminals that contacted proximal pyramidal cell dendrites.

claim: IPSCs initiated on distal dendrites have been recorded at the soma in some studies
source: However, IPSCs initiated on distal dendrites have been recorded at the soma in some studies (Silberberg and Markram, 2007; Jiang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Silberberg and Markram, 2007 and Jiang et al., 2013

claim: Differences in experimental paradigm may be responsible for differences in detecting distal dendritic IPSCs at the soma
source: Possibly differences in experimental paradigm are responsible.

claim: In this work post-synaptic potentials were more hyperpolarized (−65 mV rather than −55/−57 mV) and Cl− in the recording pipette was higher (19 rather than 10 mM) than in other studies
source: In this work post-synaptic potentials were more hyperpolarized (−65 mV rather than −55/−57 mV) and Cl− in the recording pipette was higher (19 rather than 10 mM) than in other studies.

claim: Unperturbed Cl− reversal potentials may be 10–25 mV more hyperpolarized than in invasive whole-cell recordings
source: Indeed unperturbed Cl− reversal potentials may be 10–25 mV more hyperpolarized than in invasive whole-cell recordings (Verheugen et al., 1999; Bevan et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Verheugen et al., 1999 and Bevan et al., 2000

claim: Distinct numbers and sites of synaptic contacts made by FS interneurons with pyramidal cells may be regulated by network function
source: Distinct numbers and sites of synaptic contacts made by FS interneurons with pyramidal cells may be regulated by network function (Yoshimura et al., 2005) and activity during different states (Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008; Puig et al., 2008).

claim: The strength of inhibition mediated by hippocampal FS basket cells varies with different target pyramidal cells
source: The strength of inhibition mediated by hippocampal FS basket cells varies with different target pyramidal cells.

claim: Synaptic strength is greater at connections with CA1 pyramidal cells in deep rather than superficial layers of stratum pyramidale
source: Synaptic strength is greater at connections with CA1 pyramidal cells in deep rather than superficial layers of stratum pyramidale (Lee et al., 2014) and it is genetically coded (Donato et al., 2015).

claim: Synaptic strength of FS basket cell connections is genetically coded
source: Synaptic strength is greater at connections with CA1 pyramidal cells in deep rather than superficial layers of stratum pyramidale (Lee et al., 2014) and it is genetically coded (Donato et al., 2015).

claim: The innervation patterns of cortical basket cells appear to be regulated by experience, environment or fear conditioning
source: The innervation patterns of cortical basket cells appear to be regulated by experience, environment or fear conditioning (Donato et al., 2013), according to network properties (Yoshimura et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2014) and the activity in specific target cells (Xue et al., 2014), and activity level of them may be regulated by learning as well as genetics (Donato et al., 2015).

claim: The efficacy of synapses made by Martinotti cells seems to be independent of target pyramidal cell activity

claim: Different cortical interneurons respond in distinct ways to neuronal network state

claim: Spines contacted by an inhibitory synapse are typically co-innervated by an excitatory thalamic input

claim: Single inhibitory synapses can effectively veto synaptic excitation and intercept NMDA current at the spine head

claim: Inhibitory synapses on spines could prevent summation of thalamic excitatory inputs arriving within about 20 ms

claim: Pyramidal cell and FS basket cells are co-activated by thalamo-cortical afferents
source: They could then prevent summation of thalamic excitatory inputs arriving within about 20 ms (Marlin and Carter, 2014), as pyramidal cell and FS basket cells are co-activated by thalamo-cortical afferents (Kimura et al., 2010).

claim: The FS basket cell acts as a feed forward inhibition to thalamic input
source: Hence the FS basket cell acts as a feed forward inhibition to thalamic input.

source: Excitatory synapses innervating cortical pyramidal cell spines can be modulated by visual experience (Chen et al., 2012) or by somatosensory stimulation (Knott et al., 2002).

claim: Excitatory synapses innervating cortical pyramidal cell spines can be modulated by somatosensory stimulation
source: Excitatory synapses innervating cortical pyramidal cell spines can be modulated by visual experience (Chen et al., 2012) or by somatosensory stimulation (Knott et al., 2002).

claim: The veto by inhibitory synapses terminating on spines may be especially important for plastic changes

claim: Dendritic IPSCs may exert strictly local effects

source: However this small driving force would be increased by depolarization due to dendritic EPSPs.

claim: IPSPs will reduce EPSP amplitude at the soma even if they do not propagate somatically
source: IPSPs will then reduce EPSP amplitude at the soma even if they do not propagate somatically.
